title: Process Basics
lead: Look at the running system with a microscope: what a process is, who started it and what state it is in.
objectives: You explain what a process is, what PID and PPID mean and why PID 1 is special.
You list processes with ps aux, ps -ef and ps -o, and find them with pgrep.
You show parent/child relations with pstree and ps --forest and look into /proc/<pid>.
You recognise process states (R, S, D, T, Z) and know what a zombie is and what it is not.

sections.title: What is a process?
body: A program on disk (for example `bash`) is just a file. When you start it, the kernel loads it into memory and it becomes a **process**. Hundreds of processes run at the same time.

Every process has a unique number, the **PID**. It also knows who started it: the **PPID** (parent PID). Processes give birth to each other: your shell starts `ps`, `ps` is the child of the shell. At the top is **PID 1**, the first process of the system, today usually `systemd`. All others descend from it.
The shell knows its own PID: `$$`. In the simulator it always prints 4242.

commands.what: Prints the PID of the current shell.
commands.where: In scripts and when you need your own PID, e.g. for /proc/$$.
commands.why: You can inspect your own process without searching for it.

commands.what: Lists only the processes of your current terminal.
commands.where: For a quick look: normally just `bash` and `ps` itself.
commands.why: The smallest snapshot; shows PID, terminal, CPU time and command.

sections.tip: `ps` is a **snapshot**, not a live view. For a live view you use `top` (next modules).

sections.title: Reading with ps
body: `ps` exists in two styles. `ps aux` is **BSD style** (no dash): all users, with %CPU and %MEM. `ps -ef` is **UNIX style** (with dash): all processes with a **PPID** column. `ps aux` has no PPID column; for relations use `ps -ef` or `-o`.
With `-o` you choose the columns yourself: `ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd`. This is the cleanest way for scripts and the best way to read exactly what you need.

commands.what: All processes of all users, with user, %CPU, %MEM, state and command.
commands.where: When you ask who is using the system and how much.
commands.why: Most common overview; combine with `grep` or `sort`.

commands.what: All processes in UNIX format, including the PPID column.
commands.where: When you want to know who the parent is.
commands.why: Shows relations; PPID 1 means the process hangs directly under init/systemd.

commands.what: Shows exactly the columns you list.
commands.where: In scripts and for focused questions.

commands.what: Shows only the process with the given PID.
commands.where: When you know the PID and want to check it.

sections.tip: `ps aux | grep sshd` also finds the grep process itself. `pgrep` avoids that.
sections.warn: Never rely on column positions in `ps aux` for the COMMAND field: it contains spaces. Use `ps -o` in scripts.

sections.title: Trees and searching: pstree and pgrep
body: `pstree` draws the family tree: systemd at the root, then services, your SSH session, your shell and your commands. `ps -ef --forest` shows the same with a PPID column.
`pgrep` searches by name and prints only PIDs. It is made for scripts: `pgrep -x sshd` prints the PID if `sshd` runs and exits with 1 if not.

`pstree` comes from the package `psmisc`, which is not always installed. Rocky/Alma: `sudo dnf install psmisc`. Debian/Ubuntu: `sudo apt install psmisc`. `pgrep` belongs to procps and is always there.

commands.what: Shows the process tree with PIDs.
commands.why: At a glance: everything hangs under PID 1 (systemd).

commands.what: The ps list in tree form with PPID.
commands.why: A tree plus all columns of `ps -ef`.

commands.what: Finds processes by name and prints PID and name.
commands.where: In scripts, to check whether a service runs.
commands.why: Cleaner than `ps | grep`; `-x` matches the exact name.

commands.what: Prints PID and the complete command line.
commands.where: When several processes have the same name.
commands.why: You see the arguments and can pick the right PID.

sections.tip: Package install: Rocky `sudo dnf install psmisc`, Ubuntu `sudo apt install psmisc`.

sections.title: Inside /proc/<pid>
body: `/proc` is a **virtual filesystem**: it does not live on disk, the kernel generates it. Every process has a directory `/proc/<pid>/`. That is the source `ps` itself reads from.

Useful files: `status` (name, state, PID, PPID, UID), `exe` (link to the program), `cwd` (working directory), `fd/` (open files), `cmdline` (the command line). As a normal user you can read your own processes; for others some files are restricted.
`/proc/self` always means the process that reads it. So `cat /proc/self/status` shows the status of `cat`.

commands.what: Shows name, state, PID, PPID and UID of your shell.
commands.where: For details that ps does not show.
commands.why: The raw source: State and PPid lines tell the story.

commands.what: A link to the executable of the process.
commands.where: When you ask which binary really runs.

commands.why: 0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr; more means open files.

sections.tip: `cat /proc/self/status` is a quick test that /proc works, also in WSL.

sections.title: States, zombies and signals
body: The **STAT** column shows the state: `R` running, `S` sleeping (waiting, interruptible), `D` uninterruptible sleep (usually waiting for disk/network; cannot be killed), `T` stopped (Ctrl+Z), `Z` **zombie**. Extra letters: `s` session leader, `+` foreground, `<` high priority.

A **zombie** is a process that has already finished. Only its entry in the process table remains, because the parent has not yet read the exit status (`wait`). A zombie uses no CPU and almost no memory, and **you cannot kill it, not even with `kill -9`**, because it is already dead. The fix: the parent must collect it, or you stop/restart the parent; then init adopts and reaps the orphan.

Signals: `kill` sends a signal, default `SIGTERM` (15, polite request, the program can clean up). `SIGKILL` (9) cannot be caught; the kernel ends the process immediately without cleanup. **PID 1** is special: signals without a handler are ignored for it, even SIGKILL from user space. That protects the system from an accidental kill.
Load average (`uptime`) shows runnable processes over 1/5/15 minutes. Read it **relative to the number of cores** (`nproc`): load 4.0 is full on 4 cores and overload on 2.

commands.what: All processes with state and parent.
commands.where: When looking for zombies (STAT Z) or stuck processes (D).
commands.why: Pipe to `grep` or `sort` for a quick filter.

commands.what: Shows uptime and the load average of 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
commands.where: As the first look at 'is the server slow?'.
commands.why: Compare the load with the number of cores.

commands.what: Prints the number of CPU cores.
commands.where: To read the load average correctly.
commands.why: Load 2.0 is fine on 8 cores and busy on 2.

commands.what: Sends SIGTERM (polite stop) to a PID.
commands.where: First choice to end a process.
commands.why: The program can save data and clean up.

commands.what: Sends SIGKILL; the process is ended immediately.
commands.where: Only if SIGTERM did not work.
commands.why: Last resort; no cleanup, data can be lost.

sections.tip: Order for stopping: `kill -15`, wait a few seconds, check with `ps -p PID`, and only then `kill -9`.
sections.warn: Check the PID twice before you kill. `pkill name` and `killall name` kill **all** processes with that name, including ones you did not mean.
sections.danger: Do not kill processes you do not know, especially not as root: `kill -9` on `sshd`, `systemd-journald` or a database can lock you out or corrupt data. Practise only with your own `sleep` processes.

t01.text: List the processes of your terminal with `ps`. Which two do you see?
t01.hint: Just `ps`, no options. You see `bash` and `ps`.

t02.text: Print the PID of your shell with `echo $$`.
t02.hint: Two dollar signs. In the simulator it is always 4242.

t03.text: Run the all-process view in BSD style: `ps aux`.
t03.hint: No dash for `aux`. (`ps -ef` is accepted too.)

t04.hint: Columns separated by commas, no spaces.

t05.text: Read only the header line of the snapshot with `head -n 1 ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`. Which column is the CPU usage?
t05.hint: `ps_snapshot.txt` is a saved `ps aux` output in `~/lab`. The column is %CPU.

t06.text: Show all processes of alice in the snapshot: `grep alice ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`. Which program is busy?
t06.hint: Look at the %CPU column; the process is `python3 worker.py`.

t07.text: Count the processes of alice: `grep alice ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt | wc -l`.

t08.text: Find the zombie in the snapshot with `grep defunct ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`. Which PID and which user?
t08.hint: Zombies show STAT `Z` and `<defunct>`. It is PID 1701 of bob.

t09.text: `~/lab/proc_status.txt` is a copy of `/proc/1701/status`. Find the parent: `grep PPid ~/lab/proc_status.txt`.
t09.hint: PPid is the PID of the parent; you must deal with it, not with the zombie.

t10.text: Predict first: how many lines does `ps | wc -l` print? Then run it to verify.

t11.text: Predict first: is the 1-minute load average low? Run `uptime` to verify. Remember: read load relative to `nproc`.
t11.hint: Look at the three numbers after 'load average:'.

t12.text: Sort the snapshot by CPU, highest first, and show two lines: `sort -k3 -nr ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt | head -n 2`.

t13.text: Mini project: write the PIDs of all root processes into `~/lab/root_pids.txt`. Filter with `grep ^root`, squeeze spaces with `tr -s ' '`, pick column 2 with `cut -d' ' -f2`, redirect with `>`.

t14.text: Debug: `~/lab/fix.txt` says `kill -9 1701`. That is wrong, a zombie cannot be killed. Overwrite the file with the better command: signal the parent, e.g. `kill -s SIGCHLD 1500`.
t14.hint: `echo "kill -s SIGCHLD 1500" > ~/lab/fix.txt`. The parent PID is 1500 (see t09).

t15.text: Challenge: find the process with the highest CPU usage in the snapshot using `sort`. Write the **polite** stop command for it into `~/lab/decision.txt` (do not run it).
t15.hint: It is PID 1620. Polite means signal 15: `echo "kill -15 1620" > ~/lab/decision.txt`.

t16.text: TICKET #5110 — The server is slow. Alice's job is suspected. Write the user, PID and command of the busiest process into `~/lab/report.txt`.
t16.hint: Use `sort` or `grep` on the snapshot; then `echo "alice 1620 python3 worker.py" > ~/lab/report.txt`.

t17.text: Save your shell PID to a file: `echo $$ > ~/lab/mypid.txt`.
t17.hint: `>` writes the output of `echo` into the file.

vm.intro: Run these steps on your own VM (Ubuntu, Rocky, Alma or WSL). Steps 1 to 4 only read. Step 5 stops a process: take a **snapshot** first and only touch your own `sleep` process.

v01.title: Your own process
v01.text: Print the PID of your shell, then show its PID, PPID and state with ps. Paste the output.
differs: The numbers differ on your system; `PPID` must be in the header.
In a terminal started via SSH the parent is `sshd`, in a desktop terminal it is the terminal program.

v02.title: ps aux and ps -ef
v02.text: Compare both styles. Which one has a PPID column?

blocks.expected:
USER  PID %CPU %MEM ... COMMAND
root    1  0.0  0.3 ... /usr/lib/systemd/systemd
UID   PID  PPID  C STIME TTY TIME CMD
root    1     0  0 08:00 ?   00:00:02 /usr/lib/systemd/systemd

differs: On WSL1 or in a container PID 1 may be `init` or something else.
Only `ps -ef` has PPID; `ps aux` has %CPU and %MEM.

v03.title: Process tree
v03.text: Install `psmisc` if needed and look at the tree. Who is at the root? Paste the first lines.

blocks.cmd:
# Rocky/Alma: sudo dnf install -y psmisc
# Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt install -y psmisc
pstree -p | head -n 8
ps -ef --forest | head -n 15

differs: `pstree: command not found` means psmisc is not installed; use the install line above.
On WSL you may see `init(1)` or `SessionLeader` instead of systemd.

v04.title: Look into /proc
v04.text: Read the status of your shell directly from /proc and show where the program lives.

blocks.expected:
Name:	bash
Umask:	0022
State:	S (sleeping)
...
PPid:	2050
...
lrwxrwxrwx 1 student student 0 ... /proc/2100/exe -> /usr/bin/bash

differs: The `Name:`, `State:` and `PPid:` lines must exist; the order of other lines can differ.
`exe` may show `/bin/bash` on some systems (a link to /usr/bin).

v05.title: Start and stop a process safely
v05.text: **Snapshot first.** Start your own `sleep` in the background, find it with pgrep, stop it politely with SIGTERM and check that it is gone. Never use `pkill` or `kill -9` on unknown processes.

blocks.cmd:
sleep 600 &
pgrep -l sleep
kill -15 $!
sleep 1
pgrep -l sleep || echo gone

differs: `$!` is the PID of the last background process.
If `pgrep` still prints a line, another `sleep` is running; check with `pgrep -a sleep` before you kill anything.

q1.q: Which PID has the first process of a Linux system (today usually systemd)?
q1.explain: PID 1 is started by the kernel; all other processes descend from it. It also ignores signals it has no handler for, even SIGKILL from user space.

q2.q: What is true for a zombie process (STAT Z)?
options: It uses a lot of CPU
It is finished; the parent has not collected the exit status, and `kill -9` does not help
q2.explain: A zombie is already dead; only its table entry remains. The parent must call wait, or you restart the parent.

q3.q: What does `$$` mean in the shell?
options: The PID of the current shell
The PID of the last background job
The exit code of the last command
q3.explain: `$$` is the shell's own PID. The last background PID is `$!`, the exit code is `$?`.

q4.q: Which command shows a PPID column by default?
q4.explain: `ps -ef` (UNIX style) shows PPID. `ps aux` (BSD style) does not; for it use `ps -o pid,ppid,...`.

summary: A process is a running program with a PID; its parent has the PPID; PID 1 (systemd) is the ancestor of all.
`ps aux` (BSD) shows CPU/MEM, `ps -ef` shows PPID, `ps -o` chooses columns, `pgrep` finds by name.
`pstree` (package psmisc) and `ps -ef --forest` show the tree; `/proc/<pid>` is where the kernel exposes the details.
A zombie (Z) is dead and cannot be killed; fix the parent. Use `kill -15` first, `kill -9` last, never on unknown processes.
Read the load average relative to `nproc`.

glossary.meaning: A running instance of a program with its own PID and memory.
Process ID and the ID of its parent process.
A finished process whose exit status has not yet been collected by its parent (STAT Z).
A message to a process, e.g. SIGTERM (15) or SIGKILL (9).
Virtual filesystem through which the kernel exposes process and system information.
Average number of runnable processes over 1, 5 and 15 minutes; read it relative to the CPU cores.
